Introduction
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

What is Compartment Fire?
▪ The term ‘compartment fire’ in this module is used to describe
a fire which is confined within a room or similar enclosure
within a building.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Fire Growth Stages
▪ Compartment fires are often discussed in terms of growth stages.
▪ The growth stages are:
➢ Ignition
➢ Growth
➢ Fully-developed fire
➢ Decay

OFFICIAL (OPEN)

General Description
▪ Ignition Stage:
✓ The period during which the fire begins.
▪ Growth Stage:
➢ During the initial part of growth stage, the fire grows independent of the
size, shape and material of the compartment (unless the fire and
compartment boundaries are in contact).
➢ Temperature rises are localised and escape is relatively easy.
➢ If there is sufficient fuel and oxygen, the fire will continue to grow causing
an increase in the temperature particularly in the upper part of the
compartment.
➢ Such fires which have sufficient oxygen are said to be ‘fuel-controlled.’
➢ The latter part of the developing stage generally represents the last
opportunity for escape from the compartment.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

General Description
▪ Flashover:
✓ The transition from the growth stage to the fully-developed stage.
✓ Occurs over a relatively short period.
✓ Characterised by the rapid involvement in fire of all combustible materials
within the compartment and a rapid rise in temperature.
✓ Various criteria for its onset:
a) A critical gas temperature of the upper layer of 500-600oC
b) A critical radiant heat flux at floor level of 20 kW/m2
c) The ignition of incompletely combusted material in the upper layer, or
d) The appearance of flames from openings in the compartment
*Flashover Video
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Flashover vs Backdraught
▪ There is clear distinction between flashover and backdraught.
▪ Backdraught is preceded by burning under conditions of very
poor ventilation and is initiated by the sudden influx of air
when a door opens or a window breaks.
▪ The development of flashover occurs under conditions where
a fire in a compartment already has adequate ventilation.
*Backdraught Video
Why is backdraught a concern for firefighters?
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

General Description
▪ Fully-Developed Stage:
✓ Once flashover has occurred, the fire is said to be fully developed.
✓ The Heat Release Rate (HRR) is at its maximum.
✓ Fire is generally ‘ventilation-controlled’ i.e. there is insufficient air within the
compartment, and some of the pyrolysis products will leave the
compartment, possibly to react outside the compartment.
✓ Such ‘ventilation-controlled’ fires produce large amounts of carbon
monoxide and conditions are therefore untenable for humans.
✓ The high thermal stress of the building structure and compartment
boundaries may be sufficient to cause structural damage.
✓ Spread may also occur through open doors and ducts (internal spread)
and open windows (external spread) involving adjacent enclosures in fire.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

General Description
▪ Decay Stage:
✓ After reaching a maximum rate of heat release, the fully-developed fire
begins to diminish in size as the fuel is consumed.
✓ This decay stage may be considered to commence when the average
temperature in the compartment has fallen to 80% of its peak value.
✓ The fire may change from ventilation to fuel-controlled during this period.
✓ Ultimately, the fire may cease flaming and become a smouldering mass of
glowing embers.
✓ Not of great significance as far as the safety of the occupants and
damage to the building is concerned.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Pre-Flashover Fires
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Pre-Flashover Fires
▪ In fire engineering design process, understanding
pre-flashover fire behaviour is essential when designing for
life safety in fires.
▪ The growth or pre-flashover phase is a critical phase from the point
of view of detection, escape of people, fire control and
suppression in the enclosure of origin.
▪ Once flashover has occurred, escape is unlikely and fire control is
difficult.
▪ Necessary for designer to know the expected rate of fire growth,
and the resulting temperature of the hot upper layer in the fire
room (which can be used to predict the likelihood of flashover).

Multiple Fuel Items
▪ In the practical situation, there will generally be more than one fuel
item in a compartment.
▪ The spread of fire from the item ignited first to the other items can
occur in a number of ways:
➢ Direct flame contact
➢ Radiant heat transfer
➢ By way of flashover
▪ Direct Flame Contact: If adjacent items are touching or sufficiently
close, direct flame contact can occur, and fire spread and growth
will generally be rapid. In some cases, thermoplastics materials may
facilitate spread by the formation of a flaming pool fire.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Multiple Fuel Items
▪ Ignition by Radiant Heat Transfer: Depends on the flux produced by
the item ignited first, the ignitability of the second item, the relative
geometry of the two items and the distance between them.
Experimental measurements of radiant heat flux contours generally
required.
▪ One might expect a substantial item which burns rapidly (e.g. a
polyurethane padded chair covered with a polypropylene fabric to
ignite combustible items within a radius of about a metre.)
▪ Flashover: All combustible items within the compartment become
involved in the fire. Spread of fire from one item to another may occur
indirectly through this pathway.

OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Flashover
▪ Flashover is the culmination of the growth phase and involves the
ignition of all the combustible materials in the compartment (other
than those already burning) by virtue of radiant heat.
▪ The heat may be radiated from:
➢ The flames of the developing fire
➢ The hot surfaces of the upper part of the compartment
➢ Flames under the ceiling and/or
➢ Hot combustion products in the upper layer of the compartment
▪ The relative importance of these sources of radiant heat will vary as
the fire develops and at flashover depend on a number of factors
such as the nature of the fuel and the type and degree of ventilation.
▪ For most fuels, a distinct smoky layer is produced and radiation from
this layer will predominate at flashover.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Enclosure Situations
▪ The quantity of heat radiated will depend on factors such as
the thickness of the layer, its temperature, and its emissivity.
▪ Three typical enclosure situations may be identified to illustrate
these factors.
▪ Well-Ventilated Room Fire
➢ In this scenario, the fire develops freely and establishes a well-mixed
hot layer of smoke and gases in the upper part of the room.
➢ This is the classic two-layer zone model used to study the
development of a fire to flashover.
➢ A large proportion of the heat radiated to the combustibles in the
room is from this hot layer.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Enclosure Situations
▪ A Room Fire with Reduced Ventilation
➢ In this scenario, which may occur during the latter stages of fire
development, there is retarded inflow of air and outflow of
combustion products due to the deeper layer of smoke and gases.
➢ Again, a large part of the heat radiated to the combustibles in the
lower part of the room is from the upper layer.
➢ Calculations and experimental work have indicated that, for fires
which produce considerable amounts of smoke under conditions of
restricted ventilation (e.g. polyurethane foam), up to 85% of the heat
radiated to the floor comes from the upper layer.
➢ If the rate of heat release from the fire is sufficient, the heat radiated
to the lower parts of the compartment will be sufficient (20 kW/m2 at
floor level) to cause flashover.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Enclosure Situations
▪ A Corridor
➢ For a corridor scenario with a fire at one (closed) end, the fire plume is deflected by
the ceiling to form a one-dimensional jet the depth of which will depend on the
width of the corridor and the rate of flow of hot gases into the ceiling jet.
➢ If the fire is sufficiently large, flames will enter the ceiling jet and the nature of
burning under the ceiling will depend on whether the gases comprising the ceiling
jet are ‘fuel lean’ or ‘fuel rich’.
➢ For the ‘fuel lean’ situation, there will be sufficient oxygen for combustion and the
flames in the ceiling jet will be limited in extent and burn close to the ceiling lining.
➢ For the ‘fuel rich’ situation, the flames are extended along the upper layer in the
corridor and burn at the bottom of the layer.
➢ This leads to significant increase in radiant heat flux at the floor level remote from
the fire source and increases the likelihood of flashover (and flame spread along
the corridor).
➢ As much as 55% of the heat of combustion released into the upper layer is lost by
radiation.
➢ If the ceiling lining is combustible, flame extension is further increased and the
radiant heat flux to the floor (and lower levels of the corridor) is increased
correspondingly.

OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Post-Flashover Fires
▪ The behaviour of the fire changes dramatically after flashover.
▪ The flows of air and combustion gases become very turbulent.
▪ The very high temperatures and radiant heat fluxes
throughout the room cause all exposed combustible surfaces
to pyrolyse, producing large quantities of combustible gases,
which burn where there is sufficient oxygen.
▪ The most important information for structural design is the
temperature in the room during the post-flashover fire.
▪ Post-flashover fires provide the greatest threat to structural
members and other fire-resistant building elements.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Ventilation-Controlled Burning
▪ In typical rooms, post-flashover fires are ventilation-controlled
▪ So, the rate of combustion depends on the size and shape of
ventilation openings.
▪ Usually conservatively assumed that all window glass will break
and fall out at the time of flashover (due to rapid rise in
temperature).
▪ If the glass does not fall out, the fire will burn for a longer time
at a lower rate of heat release.
▪ A fully-developed fire may be either fuel-controlled or
ventilation-controlled but in the absence of information to the
contrary, it is often assumed to be ventilation-controlled.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Fuel-Controlled Burning
▪ The rate of burning may sometimes be controlled by the surface area
of the fuel, especially in large well-ventilated rooms containing fuel
items which have a limited area of combustible surfaces.
▪ The rate of burning similar to that for fuel item burning in the open air,
with enhancement from radiant feedback from the hot upper layer
of gases or hot wall and ceiling surfaces.
▪ The rate of burning is independent of the size of the openings in the
compartment i.e. increasing the opening size does not affect the
burning, and depends particularly on the burning characteristics and
surface area of the fuel.
▪ Generally less severe; produces less hazardous combustion products
▪ Most fires become fuel-controlled in the decay period.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Wood Crib Fuel Sources
▪ Much experimental and theoretical work on fully-developed fires has used
wood cribs
▪ Provide ready means of a series of reproducible and reliable fires of many sizes
▪ Structure consists of layers of crossed sticks with air gaps between. Tends to
confine heat of combustion and facilitate cross-radiation between burning
surfaces within the crib
▪ Facilitate efficient burning of the sticks but do not generally operate in the case
of ‘real’ fuel items
▪ Burning surfaces of the crib shielded from the environment particularly from
radiation from the enclosure boundaries and any hot upper layer
▪ Rate of burning thus relatively insensitive to the thermal environment.
▪ Conclusions drawn for studies of crib fires must be applied to other fuels with
some caution.

Discarded Theories in Human Behaviour in Fires
▪ Equally important to understand what human behaviour in fires is
not as it has direct implications on the engineering design process.
▪ Three disaster myths (Panic Behaviour, Disaster Shock and Group
Mind) have been overgeneralised by society and the media to
account for negative situations in some disaster scenarios, but are
very rare in reality.
▪ They are what behaviour in an emergency does NOT look like
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Panic Behaviour
▪ Panic = “an acute fear reaction marked by loss of self-control which is
followed by non-social and non-rational flight behaviour” (Quarantelli, 1954:
272)
▪ According to Fahy, 2012, people do not usually exhibit non-social or non-
rational behaviour in emergencies:
✓ Behaviour is generally cooperative and altruistic (selfless concern for the well-being of
others), e.g., World Trade Centre, where studies of both media accounts and survivor
interviews revealed overall trends of calm and altruism
✓ Behaviour, even under stress, is relatively controlled, rational, cooperative and adaptive
▪ Panic not to be confused with anxiety or fear:
✓ E.g., “when I heard the explosion I panicked, so I grabbed the baby and ran out of the
building before it collapsed” → constructive behaviour, not panic
✓ Observers misinterpreted the state of mind of victims who misjudged resulting in fatal
consequences → may be a perfectly rational decision when faced with incomplete
information or limited options, not panic
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Effects of Stress
▪ Emergencies are time pressured, goals may shift, and there may
be little or ambiguous information
▪ Physiological (increased heart rate, blood pressure, respiration)
and emotional (tension, anxiety, fear) responses
▪ Positive: Stress increases attention, reduces distraction, irrelevant
stimuli can be a motivator to act (Klein, 1996)
▪ Negative: Evaluate smaller set of cues, consider fewer
alternatives, less systematic and can be less flexible (Janis and
Mann, 1977)
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Disaster Shock
▪ This myth creates an image of large numbers of individuals dazed or
shocked, i.e., unable to cope with the new disaster-created situation
at hand.
▪ Disaster researchers attempt to dispel this myth by explaining that
disaster response behaviour is often performed in an active manner:
✓ Instead of waiting for assistance, in a dazed or disoriented manner, disaster victims
are more likely to show considerable personal initiative, performing search and
rescue activities, casualty care, and restoration of essential services before
emergency responders arrive on scene.
▪ This kind of response was observed in the 2001 WTC disaster where
survivors were often the first individuals to respond to the needs of their
coworkers.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Group Mind
▪ Oversimplification that the group is something other than the sum
of individual responses, i.e., the group has a “mind” of its own
when making decisions in a disaster.
▪ Assumption that when a disaster occurs, individuals become a
part of a group and the group acts in response to the disaster, i.e.,
characterised as mob behaviour or herd behaviour.
▪ Making this assumption can cause the engineers to be blinded by
any diversity associated with the group, including individual
characteristics, experiences, decision-making or behaviour.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factors Influencing Behaviour in Fires
▪ People in fires very rarely act in a similar manner throughout
the fire event.
✓ Instead, based on various environmental and individual factors, they
internalise and process the information, and then act in kind.
▪ These factors include social influence (or the influence of
others in the building), stress, the built environment, leadership,
and demographics (notably gender).
Important to identify these factors so that engineers can
identify circumstances within fire scenarios in which certain
types of behaviours (resulting in time delays) are likely to occur.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 1: The Influence of Other Occupants on
Behaviour (Social Influence)
▪ Theory: One’s response behaviour (either action or inaction)
including exit choice during an emergency can be influenced
by others
▪ Evidence: “Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of
responsibility” by Darley, J.M. and Latane, B., Journal of
Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377-383.
➢ Conducted several experiments where participants were exposed to a
simulated emergency (smoke filling a room) under different groupings:
❖ Alone: 75% reported the emergency
❖ In the presence of two planted passive persons: 10% reported the emergency
Demonstrates the importance of having fire wardens lead evacuations during a fire!
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Engineering Implications of Social
Influence on Behaviour
▪ Many times, evacuation models simulate each individual as if
they are not behaviourally influenced by anyone else around
them.
✓ Not realistic. Engineers should be aware of social influence when running
simulation tools.
▪ Proper understanding of social influence can aid engineers in
developing new and more effective evacuation procedures
✓ E.g., Strategically placing fire wardens or “quick responders” throughout the
building (rather than all in one place) to promote faster response from other
building occupants
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 2: The Influence of Stress on Behaviour
(Perception)
▪ Stress can be brought on in an emergency via several
different complex conditions or states. Other than physical
harm, fires can cause other conditions of states including:
➢ Uncertainty – occurs due to missing, unreliable, ambiguous, conflicting
and/or complex information
➢ Information Overload – occurs when the individual or group perceives
that there is too much information to filter through in the time available
➢ Time Pressure – occupants perceive their situation as urgent and they only
have a limited amount of time to perform certain actions.
If individuals are more likely, in stressful situations, to pay attention to a
lower number of cues, engineers should design more noticeable signage or
warning cues that easily grab people’s attention (e.g., providing information
via luminous materials)
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 3: The Influence of the Built Environment on
Behaviour (Movement Towards the Familiar)
▪ In an emergency, people are more likely to move (evacuate)
based on what is familiar to them
▪ Evidence: “Movement toward the Familiar: Person and Place
Affiliation in a Fire Entrapment Setting” by Jonathan D. Sime,
Environment and Behavior 1985; 17; 697
➢ Based on analysis of the Summerland fire (in UK) in 1973 where 50 people
died,
❖ Majority of the staff (93%) evacuated via the exit (beside the bar) that was familiar and
commonly used by them
❖ Majority of the visitors (61%) evacuated via the entrance door which was familiar and used
by them
Demonstrates the importance of having regular fire drills!
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 3: The Influence of the Built Environment on
Behaviour (Theory of Affordances)
▪ Theory by James J. Gibson (1978): The following affordances can
explain how people perceive the things they see, which affects
the actions they take.
➢ Sensory Affordance – e.g., evacuees must be able to see an exit door/sign
➢ Cognitive Affordance – e.g., evacuees must understand what the exit sign
means and/or what the exit door is used for
➢ Physical Affordance – e.g., the exit door must be usable
➢ Functional Affordance – e.g., the exit door must help the user achieve his/her
goals, which can be subjective (e.g., getting to the carpark to retrieve the car,
returning to the mall, escaping from the fire, etc.)
Demonstrates the importance of maintaining fire safety systems, e.g., exit
signs remain lit, exit doors are usable, promoting fire safety awareness, etc.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 4: The Influence of Leadership (or Role) on
Behaviour
▪ Theory by Jones and Hewitt (IAFSS): Studied group information
and leadership during the evacuation of a high-rise office
building due to a fire.
▪ Overall, a person’s role in the organised hierarchy (pre-event
leaders) had an influence on the group actions i.e. the
leader’s group listened, relinquished decision-making to this
individual and followed directions.
▪ But when leadership failed to retain influence, new leadership
emerged i.e. even from those who were not previously in
leadership roles).
Demonstrates the importance of ensuring managers receive special fire
safety training to ensure that they are providing accurate information and
performing appropriate actions during building fires.
OFFICIAL (OPEN)

Factor 5: The Influence of Demographics
(Gender) on Behaviour
▪ Theory by Bryan (1977) and Wood(1972): Studied the influence of gender
on certain residential evacuation behaviours.
▪ Male participants were predominant in fire-fighting activities (14.9% of the
males participated in “searched for fire” as opposed to 6.3% of the
females, and 6.9% of the males were involved in the action of “got
extinguishers” as opposed to 2.8% of the females).
▪ Female participants differed significantly from the males in the warning
and evacuation activities – 11.4% of the females “called fire department”
as initial behavioural response action as opposed to 6.1% of the males.
10.4% females “left building” as the first behavioural response action
contracted with 4.2% of the males.
Demonstrates the importance for engineers to inquire how gender and
other individual-based factors influence perceptions of the threat and risk,
which then directly influence actions performed in response to a fire.
